description: Cross-binding conformance for esm-spec §6.6.4's tolerance RESOLUTION ORDER — how the `{abs?, rel?}` blocks declared at the assertion, test and model levels combine into the single `(rel, abs)` pair the §6.6.3 pass predicate is evaluated with. Resolution is PER FIELD: `abs` and `rel` are resolved independently, each taking its value from the innermost of the three declared levels that declares it, so a level declaring only one bound does not mask the other from an enclosing level. All three bindings previously returned the first non-null block WHOLE and defaulted its missing field to 0 (#228), which meant a model `{rel: 1e-6}` plus an assertion `{abs: 1e-9}` ran the assertion with NO relative bound at all. Two questions §6.6.4 left open are pinned here as well: an explicit `0` is a DECLARATION ("no bound of this kind") and stops the fallthrough, where a missing key or a JSON `null` is an ABSENCE and falls through; and the implementation default (`rel = 1e-6`, no `abs` bound) is TERMINAL — reached only when levels 1-3 declare neither bound — rather than a fourth per-field merge level.

scope_excluded.go: rewrite-only port; carries the `Tolerance` type but has no inline-test runner, so it never resolves one
scope_excluded.typescript: rewrite-only port; carries the `Tolerance` type but has no inline-test runner, so it never resolves one

integrators_note: DATA-ONLY by design. Resolution is a pure function of the declared blocks — it does not depend on a trajectory, a solver or a discretization — so this tier carries no `.esm` fixtures and pins no numeric golden. Each in-scope binding feeds `levels` straight into its `resolve_tolerance` / `_resolve_tolerance` entry point and compares the returned pair to `resolved`. That is the whole contract, and it is why this category can gate a rule that no simulating fixture could reach: every fixture in every other tier has ONE tolerance chain, so none of them distinguishes a per-field merge from a wholesale one.
absent_encoding: Within a `levels` block, a bound is DECLARED when its key is present with a number (including `0`) and ABSENT when the key is missing or its value is `null`. `esm-schema.json` types `abs`/`rel` as `number`, so a `null` is not conforming input; the `null_is_absent` case pins that a binding lenient enough to accept one treats it as an absence, which is what all three parsers already do.

cases.note: The implementation default, and the only route to it: levels 1-3 declare neither bound.
A single declared level, resolved as it always was.

THE TERMINAL-DEFAULT CONTRACT. Something was declared, so the default is out of the picture entirely — `rel` is 0, not 1e-6. Under the rejected reading in which the default is a fourth per-field merge level this case resolves to `(1e-6, 1e-3)`, and every `abs`-only assertion in the corpus silently acquires a relative bound its author never wrote.
THE DEFECT IN ITS PLAINEST FORM (#228). Before the fix every binding returned `(0, 1e-9)`: the assertion's block won wholesale and the model's relative bound vanished.
The mirror image, which pins that the merge is symmetric in the two fields and not an `abs`-only special case.
Full chain. `rel` stops at the test (the innermost level declaring it), `abs` at the assertion; the model supplies neither, because a more-specific level declared both. Before the fix: `(0, 1e-9)`.
`rel` falls past TWO levels that both decline to declare it. Before the fix: `(0, 1e-9)`.
The same masking one level up: a test declaring only `abs` used to drop its model's `rel`. Before the fix: `(0, 1e-3)`.
NON-VACUITY. A fully-specified innermost block still wins outright — the merge must not reach past a level that declares both fields.
`rel: 0` is a DECLARATION, not an absence: it is how an author says "absolute bound only" and it must block the enclosing `rel`. A binding that treated 0 as absent would resolve `1e-6` here.

The same for `abs`, at the test level. Before the fix this resolved to `(1e-6, 0)` too — the same pair by accident, because the wholesale rule zeroed the assertion's undeclared `abs` anyway. It is here for the rule, not the regression: `abs: 0` at the test must block the model's `0.1`.

EXACT EQUALITY, and the only way a document can spell it. This is what `tests/fixtures/recurrence/*.esm` declare to pin the bit-exact recurrence contract (CONFORMANCE_SPEC §5.19); a binding that read `0` as absent would silently run them at `rel = 1e-6`.

A `{}` tolerance declares neither bound, so it contributes nothing and the implementation default is reached. Before the fix a `{}` block won wholesale and produced `(0, 0)` — silent EXACT-EQUALITY mode from an empty object.
An empty block is transparent, not a barrier. Before the fix: `(0, 0)`, exact equality, from a test whose author wrote nothing at all.

A JSON `null` is not conforming input (the schema types both bounds as `number`), but a binding lenient enough to accept one MUST treat it as an absence and fall through — never as a declared 0. This is the case that separates "absent" from "explicitly 0".
